title: Mostar's Dilemma: The HVO Front Visit
sources: ICTY Prlić et al. Trial Judgment (IT-04-74-T), 29 May 2013, Herceg-Bosna command structure
ICTY Kordić & Čerkez Trial Judgment (IT-95-14/2-T), HVO organisation in central Bosnia
content:
Herceg-Bosna's leadership faced the front visit as a problem of attention divided across a war fought on two fronts at once. By 1993 the HVO was pressed against the ARBiH in central Bosnia even as it held its own lines around Mostar, and the Posavina positions in the north hung apart from the Herzegovinian heartland. A presidential appearance had to choose among them, and the choice declared a priority the rest of the front would notice. To show up was to steady the men who saw the leadership share their ground; to stay in Mostar, citing urgent diplomatic contacts with Zagreb, was to keep the political channel open at the cost of the soldier's sense of being seen.

The Prlić judgment records a Herceg-Bosna command tightly directed from Mostar and, behind it, from Zagreb — a structure in which leadership presence carried political as much as military meaning. An appearance at the central Bosnia garrisons associated the leadership with the most contested and least defensible front, where the HVO held embattled pockets among a hostile population. A visit to the Mostar front tied the leadership to the Herzegovinian core it could most plausibly hold. A turn toward the Posavina honoured the isolated northern HVO at the price of signalling that Mostar's eyes were elsewhere.

Each variant carries its own shadow. The gesture that steadies a garrison can also expose how exposed that garrison is; the press visit that wins sympathy abroad spends command focus to get it; the decision to remain in Mostar protects the Zagreb channel but lets the line read the leadership's absence as indifference. For Herceg-Bosna, whose legitimacy was itself contested, the optics of presence were never separable from the optics of the project it served.

This is a recurring leadership gesture rather than a documented single trip, and the Codex holds the most recent choice. It moves morale, cohesion, and standing, not the map. The honest reading is that an HVO front visit could rally a strained command or merely dramatise a strain the leadership could not resolve — and that for a contested authority, even genuine solidarity was watched for what it admitted.
